The Story of Dharmasinh Muni

I bow to Lord Jinendra, who is worshipped and praised by gods of all types and is an ocean of knowledge, and I write the story of Dharmasinh Muni.

King Veersen of Kaushalnagar in the southern land and Queen Veermati had two children — a son named Chandrabhuti and a daughter named Chandrashri. Chandrashri was very beautiful. Her beauty was such that it captivated all who saw her.

Chandrashri was married to King Dharmasinh of Kaushal city in the Kaushal region. The couple lived happily. Various objects of sensual pleasure were always available to them. Despite all this, the king had complete faith in dharma and boundless devotion. He always practised charity, worship, vows, and other religious duties.

One day, Dharmasinh went to see the ascetic Damdhar Muni. With devotion, he worshipped and praised the monk and heard his sacred discourse on dharma — the dharma that is worshipped with great devotion even by the gods. The discourse had a deep effect on Dharmasinh's mind. He became detached from the world and sensual pleasures. His queen Chandrashri was greatly distressed at his decision to take initiation in his youth. But the poor woman was helpless. When her brother Chandrabhuti learned of her grief, he too was deeply saddened. He could not bear to see his sister in this state. So he forcibly brought Dharmasinh back from the meditation grove and kept him with Chandrashri.

But Dharmasinh did not stay. He went away again and took initiation once more, practising great austerities. One day, while he was meditating, he saw Chandrabhuti coming toward him. He understood that this man would again disrupt his meditation. So to protect his meditation, he entered the body of a dead elephant lying nearby, took samadhi, and at the end, left his body and went to heaven. Therefore, worthy souls should protect their vows even in times of hardship, so that they may attain the supreme happiness of heaven or liberation.

May the pure Jain dharma-loving Shri Dharmasinh Muni, who took refuge in the path of austerity that bestows heaven and liberation through the teaching of Lord Jina, and who through the merit of that practice attained heavenly happiness — may that great soul, famous in the world and illuminating the intellect of all through his virtues, grant me auspicious happiness.

This story teaches that the protection of one's spiritual vows is of supreme importance, even in the face of worldly pressure. King Dharmasinh was pulled away from his monastic life by his brother-in-law's force, but he did not give up. He took initiation again and protected his meditation even at the cost of leaving his body. The wise should understand that worldly relationships, however dear, should never be allowed to obstruct the path to liberation.
